lesson.title: One Seat Each First: How Electrons Spread Out Before Pairing Up
lesson.summary: Hund's rule states that electrons fill degenerate orbitals within a subshell one at a time, all with parallel spin, before any orbital receives a second electron, because spreading out minimizes electron-electron repulsion.
lesson.body:
Suppose you need to place three electrons into a p subshell, which you already know is made of three separate orbitals, px, py, and pz, all at the same energy. The Aufbau principle tells you those three electrons belong in the 2p subshell rather than somewhere higher, and the Pauli exclusion principle tells you no single orbital can hold more than two electrons. Neither rule, on its own, tells you whether the three electrons should crowd two into one orbital and leave the third electron alone, or spread out one per orbital. That is the gap Hund's rule fills.

Friedrich Hund's rule states that when electrons occupy degenerate orbitals, orbitals of equal energy within the same subshell, they fill each orbital singly first, with parallel (same direction) spins, before any orbital receives a second electron. Only once every orbital in the subshell already has one electron does pairing begin, and pairing always requires the second electron in a given orbital to flip to the opposite spin, since the Pauli exclusion principle demands that. The physical reason is straightforward: electrons repel each other because they carry the same negative charge, and two electrons crammed into the same small orbital experience much more repulsion than two electrons sitting in separate, more spread out orbitals. Parallel spins in separate orbitals also come with a small additional stabilization called exchange energy, which favors keeping electrons unpaired when possible.

Nitrogen is the standard worked example. Nitrogen has atomic number 7, giving the configuration 1s2 2s2 2p3. The first four electrons fill 1s and 2s completely, leaving three electrons for the three 2p orbitals. Hund's rule says those three electrons do not pair up in px while leaving py and pz empty; instead, one electron goes into px, one into py, and one into pz, each with the same spin direction, leaving all three 2p orbitals singly occupied and all three electrons unpaired. Only when a fourth 2p electron arrives, as it does in oxygen, does pairing begin, forcing one orbital to hold two electrons with opposite spins while the other two orbitals stay singly occupied.

You can check this against oxygen directly, since you already worked out its configuration as 1s2 2s2 2p4. Distributing those four 2p electrons under Hund's rule gives px with two electrons (paired, opposite spins) and py and pz with one electron each (unpaired). That leaves oxygen with two unpaired electrons overall, a detail that is not just bookkeeping trivia: unpaired electron count determines whether a substance is paramagnetic, weakly attracted into a magnetic field, and it directly predicts the fact that oxygen gas is indeed paramagnetic, a property you can actually observe in a lab by pouring liquid oxygen near a strong magnet.

Hund's rule, the Pauli exclusion principle, and the Aufbau principle work as a single coordinated procedure rather than three unrelated facts to memorize separately. Aufbau tells you which subshell to fill next; Pauli sets the two electron ceiling on each individual orbital; Hund's rule tells you how to distribute electrons among the multiple orbitals of one subshell before pairing kicks in. Every electron configuration and every orbital diagram you draw from here forward, including the ones you will use to identify valence and core electrons, rests on applying all three together.
